title: Near or Distant? Elite Climate Rhetoric and Public Opinion in Ireland
text:
Near or Distant? Elite Climate Rhetoric and Public Opinion in Ireland
    
            with
                                    James P. Cross.
                            
        
    [Pre-registered]
    
    
    
        
    
    
    
        Abstract
        Elite rhetoric varies systematically in how near or distant it portrays climate impacts. This pre-registered two-stage survey experiment, fielded to a nationally representative panel of adults in Ireland, tests how such portrayals, in messages attributed to Members of the European Parliament, affect public climate opinion. Stage 1 is a between-subjects framing experiment that estimates the effect of a near versus distant portrayal of climate change on support for mitigation policy, registered as an equivalence test given the small effects reported in prior work. Stage 2 is a forced-choice conjoint that decomposes which framing features (discussing impacts, describing them specifically, and locating them proximately) and which messenger attributes (gender, political position and nationality) shape perceived persuasiveness.

title: Here and Now or There and Then? The Psychological Distance of Climate Change in Parliamentary Speech
text:
Here and Now or There and Then? The Psychological Distance of Climate Change in Parliamentary Speech
    
        
    [Under Review]
    
    
    
        
    
    
    
        Abstract
        When politicians describe climate change as a threat to future generations in faraway places, they render it abstract; when they speak of floods at home and livelihoods at stake today, they bring it close. Experimental research shows this distinction matters: proximate framing increases concern and support for action, but these literatures rarely speak to each other. What determines whether a legislator chooses to proximise? I address this question using over 35,000 European Parliament speeches from 2014 to 2024, classifying whether legislators mention environmental impacts, frame them as specific or universal, and situate them as proximate or distant. Gender and left-right ideology emerge as the most consistent predictors: female and left-leaning legislators discuss impacts more frequently and frame them as closer. Legislators respond to domestic climate salience, but EU integration position does not shape climate rhetoric. The paper shows that generative language models can efficiently label training data for fine-tuned classifiers.

title: A Heuristic Method for Automatic Gaze Detection in Constrained Multi-Modal Dialogue Corpora
text:
A Heuristic Method for Automatic Gaze Detection in Constrained Multi-Modal Dialogue Corpora
    
            with
                                    Maria Koutsombogera                                                and Carl Vogel
                                            
        
    
    PaperOpen AccessSource Code
    
    
        
    
    




Abstract
We describe a heuristic-based approach to determining gaze allocation automatically in a multi-modal task oriented dialogue corpus. We present the development of the system and the evaluation of its performance and discuss the findings, including the shortcomings and the perspectives of the implemented approach.

title: CodeBook Studio
text:
CodeBook Studio
    
        
    
    AppDocumentation
    
    
        
    
    



CodeBook Studio is a browser-based text annotation tool for computational social science. Researchers define an annotation task once — with sections, instructions, examples, tooltips, and response formats — annotate texts in the browser, adjudicate unresolved coder disagreements, and export the codebook and labelled data for downstream use, including systematic LLM benchmarking in CodeBook Lab.

Checkbox, dropdown, Likert-scale, textbox, and span-style annotation types
Codebook editor with integrated instructions, examples, and live annotation preview
Consistent annotation interface for teams of coders
Codebook export in JSON, LaTeX, and Markdown for papers and appendices
Adjudication mode for completing unresolved labels from CodeBook Lab queues
Version comparison for checking changes between codebook drafts
LLM prompt preview for checking how the task will be presented to models
CSV input and output for interoperability

For a full guide to CodeBook Studio’s features, see the CodeBook Studio documentation.
The app is available at codebook.streamlit.app. Citation details for CodeBook Studio are available on the CodeBook citation page.

title: Lorcan McLaren
text:
I am a PhD researcher in computational social science at University College Dublin, funded by a Taighde Éireann – Research Ireland Government of Ireland scholarship, and based in the Connected_Politics Lab under the supervision of James P. Cross. My research focuses on political communication, climate politics and public opinion, combining text-as-data methods, large language models and survey experiments. I also work on best practice for LLM-based text annotation and develop open-source tools for it.
Prior to my doctoral studies, I completed a BA in Computer Science, Linguistics and French at Trinity College Dublin and an MSc in Politics and Data Science at University College Dublin, complemented by two years of industry experience as a data analyst.
I will be on the academic job market in 2027, for positions starting in the 2027/28 academic year.

title: Lorcan McLaren
text:
Research

Working Papers


    
        
        When Climate Change Hits Home: Extreme Weather and Climate Rhetoric in the European Parliament
        
    [Draft Available]
    Abstract
    
    
        Climate change is often understood as a psychologically distant threat. This paper asks whether extreme weather near a politician’s geographic home changes how climate impacts are described in parliamentary speech. I combine sentence-level annotations of 28,448 European Parliament speeches with two exposure registers: a meteorological record of locally unusual warm spells and a disaster impact register of recorded floods, storms, and other climate-related events. Both are analysed at the MEP-speech-day level using three adjacent 30-day pre-speech windows, a 30-day future-exposure placebo, MEP and calendar-date fixed effects, and country-clustered inference. The primary meteorological estimate is small and statistically indistinguishable from zero (0.059 percentage points; p = 0.151); its 90% confidence interval excludes effects larger than 0.026 outcome standard deviations. The summer-heat specification is also null. In the disaster register, the primary occurrence-and-impact dose combines event frequency with the logged number of people affected and killed. Its immediate proximity estimate is positive but uncertain (0.060 percentage points; clustered p = 0.099; wild-cluster p = 0.112), with an equivalence bound of 0.024 outcome standard deviations. An unweighted event-count robustness is nominally significant (p = 0.030) but does not survive adjustment across temporal windows. The evidence rules out large changes in elite climate framing and provides limited evidence of a small immediate association following nearby recorded disasters.
    
    
    
    
    

    

    
        
        What to Compare and When to Stop: LLM Pipelines for Text Annotation in Political Science
        with James P. Cross, Zuzanna Krakowska, Robin Rauner and Martijn Schoonvelde.
    [Revise & Resubmit, Political Analysis]
    AbstractPreprint
    
    
        Political scientists increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to annotate text. Model, prompt, and inference choices can alter results and create researcher degrees of freedom. We ask how researchers can choose a defensible annotation pipeline without testing every configuration. We vary model choice and prompting condition across political science annotation tasks, using open-weight LLMs. Separate within-family comparisons examine model size. We hold hardware constant and freeze each task’s codebook. We then simulate selection strategies using human-coded validation data and evaluate selected pipelines on held-out texts. After the task itself, task–model interaction explains the largest share of performance variation. Overall model rankings are poor indicators of performance for a particular codebook. Prompting has little average effect but can substantially change performance for individual model–task combinations. Validation can screen out weak pipelines but often cannot identify a unique best one. Testing shortlisted models zero-shot yields nearly the same held-out performance as exhaustive search, with much less energy. We recommend screen-then-expand: stop when the study’s pre-set performance threshold is met, then select the most efficient configuration within a pre-set margin of the best validation score. We also propose annotation-specific reporting standards. Accompanying open-source tools support codebook development and pipeline benchmarking.

title: CodeBook Lab
text:
CodeBook Lab
    
        
    
    Python PackageDocumentation
    
    
        
    
    



CodeBook Lab is a Python package for running validation-first LLM annotation experiments against human-coded benchmark data. It takes a codebook.json and labelled ground-truth.csv exported from CodeBook Studio, removes human labels before annotation, and scores model outputs against the held-out labels.
Researchers can evaluate local Ollama models systematically across the dimensions that matter for text-as-data research:

Model choice and model size: compare any locally available Ollama models
Prompt style and example use: compare standard, persona, and chain-of-thought wrappers with or without codebook examples
Chat and reasoning modes: test fresh chats per query, per-text chats, continuous chats, and model reasoning settings
Sampling settings: sweep over temperature, top-p, and related generation parameters

Experiments are controlled from Python, so users can start with a single run, scale up to multiple experiment specifications, or iterate through larger parameter grids when needed. Because the codebook and labelled data stay constant across runs, each configuration can be compared against the same human labels.



  
    CodeBook Studio
    
      Define the annotation task
      Annotate texts with humans
      Export codebook.json and ground-truth.csv
    
  

  →

  
    CodeBook Lab
    
      Run LLM annotation experiments
      Isolate model, prompt, chat, reasoning, and sampling effects
      Score outputs against human labels
    
  

  
    
      Shared inputs
      codebook.json + human-annotated ground-truth.csv
    

    →

    
      Experiment outputs
      Accuracy, agreement, runtime, energy, and emissions metrics
    
  

CodeBook Lab also supports human-reliability workflows: it can validate coder CSVs, calculate inter-coder agreement, identify unresolved disagreements, and build an adjudication queue that can be completed in CodeBook Studio. Final outputs include run-level annotation quality, runtime, prompt and response length, energy consumption, and estimated carbon emissions, with aggregate metrics logged for cross-experiment comparison.
The package ships with a bundled starter task so you can test the workflow before plugging in your own data. For installation, experiments, human reliability, and the full API, see the CodeBook Lab documentation. Citation details for both CodeBook Lab and CodeBook Studio are available on the CodeBook citation page.
Full package documentation is available at lorcanmclaren.com/codebook-lab.

title: Gaze, Dominance and Dialogue Role in the MULTISIMO Corpus
text:
Gaze, Dominance and Dialogue Role in the MULTISIMO Corpus
    
            with
                                    Maria Koutsombogera                                                and Carl Vogel
                                            
        
    
    PaperOpen Access
    
    
        
    
    




Abstract
Analysis of human interactions benefits from understanding patterns of gaze in dialogue. Using a multi-modal task oriented dialogue corpus, we evaluate relations between gaze behaviours, conversational dominance and dialogue role. Dominant players spend more time looking at their co-player than their less dominant fellows; the facilitator spends more time gazing at the dominant player than at the less dominant; dominant players spend longer averting their gaze than their less dominant fellows. When aligned with dialogue roles, gaze behaviour differences between players are demonstrated when occupying the role of speaker but not of listener. Less dominant speakers gaze longer at a facilitator, while effects on averted gaze and co-player directed gaze remain present for dominant speakers but not for dominant listeners. Finally, where dominance is not balanced among players, mutual gaze involving players only is less than mutual gaze involving facilitators.
